speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In light of the recent confirmation by a group of Portuguese officers of the earlier accounts by Catholic priests of the massacre of civilians by Portuguese colonial

troops in Mozambique, will the Secretary of State for External Affairs take the opportunity to repeat to Portugal, an ally of Canada in NATO, our abhorrence of the repression of the remnants of the Portuguese colonial empire in Africa and will he urge Portugal once again to grant freedom to the independence movements in these areas?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the first part of the question, I have no independent confirmation of the reports on the radio this morning. I should like to say, however, that Portugal clearly must be held responsible for any such atrocities committed by their forces against innocent civilians in those African territories. First, I have urged the Portuguese foreign minister, and I will do so again whenever I have the opportunity, to negotiate with the liberation movements for the independence of the colonial territories. subsubtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOREIGN ENCROACHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I began my remarks shortly before ten o'clock last night, I had referred to what I thought was a rather misleading statement by the minister when he said we have no professional baseball in Canada and that, therefore, he and the government would not necessarily have to be concerned about baseball. We have many semi-professional baseball teams across the country. Attempts are being made to establish leagues in Canada. The main difficulty in respect of baseball in Canada is in attracting people to watch the game. This has been a severe problem in the city of Calgary where I know many people have attempted to
April 23, 1974

establish a semi-professional league. At the present time the game does not have sufficient drawing power to attract great audiences. However, it might do so some day. We might be able to entice Americans to come up here to play baseball and thereby encourage Canadians by providing them with an opportunity to learn from the best there is in the business. This is one aspect of football. Over the years we have encouraged American players to play football in Canada so that we could learn from them, the best in the business. Many of our young players have gone to United States colleges to learn to play football and then returned to Canada. It is true that a few remain in the United States to play football there.
I was quite disappointed when I read the speech of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming). I had thought he was a long-time admirer of the former leader of the Liberal party, Mr. Pearson. However, it seemed to me that he was preaching for a cause which was not necessarily football but rather a personal cause within the Liberal party. Certainly Mr. Pearson, well known by many people to have been a great admirer of sports, would have been very hesitant to put his stamp of approval upon the minister's legislation. But this government, of course, is doing a number of things the former Liberal government would never have done.
The hon. member for York West stated that he had received communications from the various mayors across Canada. He did not include Mayor Drapeau of Montreal among those. The minister, in closing his speech during the debate, said that this bill will go to the committee and that the committee will be at liberty to call all the witnesses it wishes. Well, in respect of the Bill C-18 concerning oil, the committee was told there was a desire to get the bill back into the House the next week and, therefore, it was hardly possible to call witnesses. This question perhaps has been better aired and maybe witnesses would be prepared to appear before the committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to discuss the pros and cons of the Toronto Northmen operating in Toronto or in Buffalo or in Seattle. Surely, among the witnesses who should be called are the COJO people from Montreal or Mayor Drapeau, because Montreal generally gets what Montreal wants. We should know exactly what it wants so that we can support or not support this bill from the proper outlook one might form here in Ottawa.
Let us take a look at football itself. The Canadian game of football was originally called rugger. An article which appeared in the Globe and Mail for April 17 says that rugby football originated in England. This game has been changed and somewhat modified. We have adopted the American rules. We took the forward pass and we used American imports. Even the scoring system was changed to correspond with the system in the United States. A touchdown originally counted for five points, but we increased it to six points to correspond with the value of a touchdown in the United States. It is said in this article that the west was the first to use American imports. It goes on to mention Fritz Hansen. I knew Fritz Hansen but did not know he was an American. Certainly, many Americans have come to Canada to play football and have remained in Canada.
Canadian Professional Football
The minister has no precedent for this particular piece of legislation. He mentioned that the Grey Cup game is a great national event for all Canadians. It has been said that this event stimulates an interest in sports, that it has become symbolic of athletic competition because it brings east and west together and thereby contributes to the unity of the nation. If the minister wants to bring together east and west he could make a contribution to the eastern part of Canada. He does not seem to be doing anything to encourage the playing of football in the maritimes. He does nothing to subsidize a team in St. John's, Newfoundland. That is where hockey is presently taking over. The people love the game. I am sure there are many people there who would like to play football and have the benefit of the salaries paid by the CFL or the WFL. I do not see Mr. Lalonde giving any help to teams in St. John's, Halifax or to any other Canadian team.
The minister goes on to say that without denigrating the value of free enterprise, even its most vocal proponents would concede that government must be prepared to intervene on occasion to protect the legitimate interest of all Canadians. Then, it is stated that various actions have been taken by the Canadian Government to control the operations of numerous aspects of the private sector, such as in banking, foreign investment, broadcasting, and communications. Well, it is nice I suppose for the football players to realize they are part of that eminent group of bankers, broadcasters and communicators, but certainly we must ask what we are doing for the young Canadian who wants to play ball and get paid the best money possible. Recently reference has been made in the newspapers to the Toronto Northmen signing three players from the Miami Dolphins. In addition, however, they signed up a Canadian boy named Stevenson from Edmonton. I do not think the Edmonton Eskimos could pay him enough. Who would say that young Stevenson should not accept more money from the Toronto Northmen? I do not believe any thinking Canadian would blame Stevenson for taking more money from the Toronto Northmen to play in that league. Why should he not do so? His athletic career will last only a few years and he should get the money while he can.
Mr. Lalonde made a few erroneous statements-

speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker. I was referring to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He made a number of erroneous statements. Apparently the minister said on a radio program that the World Football League would go after CFL players even if the Northmen were allowed to operate in Canada, and the World Football League would probably set up teams in Montreal and Vancouver. The Minister knows full well that he has had an offer of a written guarantee from the Toronto Northmen to the effect that if they are allowed to operate in Toronto they will honour the CFL contract, and will in no way attempt to raid the CFL, except, when a contract on a player's option was available.

April 23, 1974
Canadian Professional Football
The minister also knows full well that if the Toronto Northmen were allowed to operate in Toronto the government would then have the determination as to whether or not there would be another world football team operating in Canada because Mr. Bassett has that franchise and is prepared to turn it over to the government or to the CFL, whichever the government felt would be better. The Northmen have also offered to make payments for the next ten years that will equal the payments the Argonauts have made into the equalization fund in 1973.
It has been said that the Regina team sorely needs these equalization payments. If one wanted to look at their books one would find that their operation has been rather a success financially. I am not saying that they are as well off as they would want to be, nor am I saying that they are rolling in cash, but they are far sounder as a financial enterprise than are the Montreal Alouettes. The Canadian Football League has sent every member of the House their blue brochure which outlines the average payments of the Argonauts which have been $55,000. I do not think that $55,000 divided into eighteen will make or break the Canadian Football League. The people in Regina to whom I spoke on this matter said that their big problem is to fill Taylor field with spectators. We will fill Taylor field with spectators if we provide them with a good brand of football and if the economy of the local citizens allows them to pay the price of the tickets. I do not think they will have any trouble maintaining the Regina football team. If the economy worsens so far as grain prices are concerned, Taylor field might have difficulties. If the Regina team does not find successful replacements for their all star quarterback and their running back, then they may have trouble filling Taylor field.
But it will not matter what happens in Toronto because Mr. Bassett and the Northmen have also promised not to televise the games of the World Football League anywhere in Canada. That is a bigger commitment than they are prepared to make if they have to move to Buffalo. If they move to Buffalo, CTV already has a contract with them to televise their games in Toronto. The amazing thing is that even though the Toronto Northmen will be operating in Buffalo, the fact they are owned by Canadians will allow compliance with the Canadian content rule of our broadcasting system, so their games can be broadcast in Canada if they are forced to move out of Toronto. It seems to me that it will be more detrimental to filling Taylor field in Regina if I, or a person in or near Regina, can sit at home and watch the World Football League on television. It may not be a Canadian team, but it will be owned by Canadians and may have Canadian players on it, so we may be more content to sit at home and watch that game than pay the price of a ticket to watch a game in Taylor field.
So it seems to me that Bill C-22, rather than helping the Canadian Football League, is in fact doing it harm. It will be detrimental to the Canadian Football League if the Toronto Northmen have to move out of Canada. If they are allowed to remain in Canada, it may be difficult for the Toronto Argonauts, but if there is no broadcasting of the games in Canada the other teams will not hurt, provided the Northmen live up to their commitment that they will make the equalization payments the Toronto Argonauts

have made. The book I have here says that last year the Toronto Argonauts paid $50,000 in equalization payments, and the average payment has been $55,000. I do not think the Northmen will quibble about the other $5,000, but they are serious and they will have a team on the World Football League. The World Football League will become an empire.
If they are forced to go to the United States then, as they have said publicly, they will openly raid the CFL, and the CFL will be in severe danger. There will be far more Stevenson's who will opt to go for the higher money. Stevenson, from Edmonton, had a perfect opportunity; he was breaking into professional football. Born in Edmonton, he went to the United States to learn how to play the game. He was offered big money and went for it. There will be all kinds of American players now playing in CFL who will, in fact, be offered contracts and no attention will be paid to their existing contracts. Jack Gotta, the former coach of Ottawa Roughriders, has stated that he would not mind having five members of the Grey Cup champions, the Ottawa Roughriders, on his team in Alabama. I suppose he would be prepared to pay somewhat more than they are getting up here, and he knows exactly what they are getting here having been their coach. If we want to help the CFL in Canada, then every member of the House should defeat this bill, but if we want to kill the sport and kill the hopes and aspirations of many young Canadians who believe that through sports they can achieve their fame, then we should support this bill.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has never been much of an athlete or he would not have put this bill before the House. I know nothing of his past but I judge the man by his attempts to stifle sports in Canada and I am very disappointed in his attitude to that matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING EXPORT OF NATURAL RESOURCE PRODUCTS AND LIMITATION OF IMPORT OF FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
that Bill C-4, to amend the Export and Import Permits Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said; Mr. Speaker, in introducing this bill for second reading, it is my intention to outline the basic reasons for proposing the amendments to the Export and Import Permits Act as set out in the measure before us. As I am pinch-hitting for my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), who will be returning tomorrow from a trade mission, I shall confine my remarks to the fundamental objectives of the bill and try to be as brief as possible. We can go into detail while in committee to whatever extent may be necessary.
Under the terms of the Export and Import Permits Act, the Governor in Council may establish a list of goods called an "export control list" whereby the export of any article can be made subject to control for certain purposes as specified in section three of the act. The first objective of the bill is to add the following two purposes to those already set out in section three:
to ensure that any action taken to promote the further processing in Canada of a natural resource which is produced in Canada is not rendered ineffective by reason of the unrestricted exportation of that natural resource;
to limit or keep under surveillance the export of any raw or processed material which is produced in Canada in circumstances of surplus supply and depressed prices and which is not a produce of agriculture.
Under section five of the same act, the Governor in Council may also establish a list of goods, called an "import control list", whereby the import of any article may be made subject to control for certain purposes as specified in that section.
The second objective of Bill C-4 is to add the following purpose to those for which imports can be made subject to control;

April 23, 1974
Export and Import Permits
to restrict, for the purpose of supporting any action taken under the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act, the importation in any form of a like article to one produced or marketed in Canada the quantities of which are fixed or determined under that act.
The third objective of Bill C-4 is to repeal section 27 of the Export and Import Permits Act setting out the expiry date of the act.
The first point I would draw to the attention of the House is that, apart from the deletion of the expiry date, the proposed amendments constitute enabling legislation. The fundamental concern of the government in respect of both the proposed amendments is to establish further purposes for which products can be placed on the export control list to ensure to the maximum extent possible that proper economic advantage is derived from raw or processed materials produced in Canada.
The object of the amendment to enable the Governor in Council to place items on the export control list in order to promote further processing of a natural resource produced in Canada is self-evident from the wording. The amendment will provide one of the means which may be needed to promote the processing of resources in Canada in cases where such processing can be internationally competitive and consistent with sound industrial structure. This is not to imply that the most desirable or the most effective way to encourage the processing of resources is by introducing export controls. Quite the contrary. The government's general approach is to focus on constructive co-operative tools such as multilateral trade negotiations, taxation policy, existing programs of industrial support, consultation with industry and the foreign investment review process. Nevertheless, it is conceivable an occasion might arise when, despite such positive efforts or in conjunction with them, it might be necessary to make the exportation of some natural resources subject to control if further processing in Canada is desirable and is to be achieved.
The object of the proposed amendment to limit or keep under surveillance the export of raw or processed materials produced in Canada in circumstances of surplus supply is to establish a provision which can be used, if needed, to ensure that proper economic advantage is derived from raw or processed materials produced in this country. Occasions may arise when Canada possesses a particular material in abundance, as well as an influential place in the international market with respect to its price. In such circumstances, over-supply from Canadian sources could result in reducing prices or holding them at an inappropriately low level having regard to such factors as the capital invested in production, the long term need, and the future value of the material involved. In this situation, various steps to promote appropriate pricing might be possible; for example, international or national co-operative marketing arrangements. However, one advisable step might be to make the material in question subject to export control for a time. The proposed amendment in respect of material in surplus supply would make it possible to initiate such action and to do so with a promptness which would yield best results.
Hon. members will have noted that agricultural products are excluded from the amendment dealing with materials in surplus supply. The reason is that there are no situations involving products, other than those already under the control of the Canadian Wheat Board, in which

Canada would have the necessary strength in world markets to influence the price of a commodity through unilateral export restriction.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to turn to the proposed amendment aimed at establishing an additional purpose for which imports can be made subject to control. The amendment is as follows:
to restrict, for the purpose of supporting any action taken under the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act, the importation in any form of a like article to one produced or marketed in Canada the quantities of which are fixed or determined under that act.
As hon. members know, the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act, which became law in 1972, allowed for the creation of national farm marketing agencies to promote strong, efficient and competitive industries having due regard to the interests of producers and consumers. To date, such agencies have been established to deal with eggs and turkeys. Under the act, agencies have the power-in respect of eggs and poultry only-to determine quantities which may be marketed in interprovincial and export trade by setting production or marketing quotas.
It is possible that in future a supply-management program of this kind could be undermined, on occasion, by an influx, or the threat of an influx, of low priced products, particularly from other countries. Therefore, it is being proposed to permit the application of import controls, if required, to support the operation of national supply-management programs for eggs and poultry. This is not to imply, of course, that it would be the intention of the government, if it did decide to apply import controls on eggs or poultry for a particular period, to attempt to insulate the Canadian market for these products for longterm trends in international prices.
One point to which I should like to draw the attention of the House is that, if this amendment is enacted, it does not mean that an agricultural product will be automatically added to the import control list because a supply-management program is being implemented under the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. In fact, if the authorities concerned under this act believe that a particular product should be added to the import control list to complement a particular supply-management program, they will have to make a specific recommendation to this effect. Then, the government will, of course, examine the case and decide whether or not to recommend to the governor in council the desired addition to the import control list, as well as establish the duration and conditions under which import controls will be exercised for the particular product or products in question.
Finally, Bill C-4 proposes the repeal of Section 27 of the Export and Import Permits Act which states that "This Act shall expire on the 31st day of July, 1974". The act, which was enacted in 1947, has been repeatedly extended. The last extension, which established the existing expiry date, took place in 1969.
It is proposed to repeal Section 27 since the inclusion of an expiry date in what is, in effect, ongoing enabling legislation, is, first, inconsistent with the fact that the act was intended to implement various international commitments, as well as complement other acts of parliament

which are not subject to expiry dates; and, second, leads to unnecessary administrative expense both for industry and government departments, as well as introduces an element of uncertainty in private companies' export sales efforts on long lead-time delivery items in contracts with certain potential purchasers. As hon. members appreciate, the repeal of Section 27 would simply mean that the act's continued existence is at the pleasure of parliament.
Canada has various ongoing international commitments that are implemented under the Export and Import Permits Act which are not subject to expiry dates corresponding to the limited duration of the act, the time and extension of which I just described. These include export control commitments in respect of military equipment and strategic supply; controlling trade, for instance, with Rhodesia in keeping with the United Nations' resolutions on Rhodesia; implementing international commodity control commitments, for example on cocoa; and administering cross-border arrangements with the United States to facilitate Canadian trade. The act is also used on an ongoing basis, as required, to complement action initiated by agencies named in Section 5(b), that is the Agricultural Stabilization Act, the Fisheries Prices Support Act, the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act, the Agricultural Products Board Act, and the Canadian Dairy Commission Act. None of these five acts contain an expiry date. In addition, the Export and Import Permits Act is used on a continuing basis for implementing import controls which are deemed necessary as a result of recommendations to the government made under the Anti-Dumping and Textile and Clothing Board Acts.
In referring to the various other acts for which the Export and Import Permits Act may provide complementary support, perhaps I should mention at this time that the act does not, of course, include any provisions, nor are any provisions being proposed, whereby items are automatically added to the import control list or export control list at any time as a result of action initiated under any other act. When items are added or deleted from the import or export control list, the government takes and must continue to take a decision in each case having regard to its international commitments and the recommendations which may be made to it by departments, agencies or boards, as well as whatever other significant circumstances prevail at the time.
I might add also that the Canadian Dairy Commission Act is the only act of the group of five named in subsection 5(b) for which the Export and Import Permits Act is being used to provide complementary support at the present time. In this connection, 10 products are on the import control list: Animal feeds containing more than 40 per cent of non-fat milk solids, butter, certain butterfats, cheese of all types, dry buttermilk, dry casein and caseinates, dry skimmed milk, dry whole milk, dry whey and evaporated and condensed milks.
The inclusion of an expiry date in the act leads, as I said, to unnecessary administrative expense for industry and government departments. For example, it is customary practice to issue export permits covering a six-month period to reduce the work of applying and issuance to a minimum. However, once the act approaches its expiry date, as is the present situation, this economizing of effort
Export and Import Permits
cannot be achieved so that additional applications must be filed and processed this year.
Another example is that it is customary to issue certain export permits for periods of one year for aircraft replacement parts in cases where companies have specific ongoing commitments to export items on an urgent rush basis in order that aircraft will only be grounded for a minimum length of time but, during the calendar year in which the act is due to expire, the business of arranging these special permits must be done twice. The same situation does exist, as a matter of fact, in respect of approximately 400 special calendar year export permits which have been issued to logging and pulpwood firms. Similar difficulty is being encountered on the import control list side in respect of shirts, where approximately 65 importing companies are involved.
An expiry date in the act can also introduce an element of uncertainty in private companies' export sales negotiations with potential purchasers, particularly in countries which are on the area control list. State-trading countries are accustomed to obtaining export permits and, indeed, in most cases, require that a permit be issued to cover a long-lead delivery item before completion of a final sales contract. Cases have arisen, however, where it has been impossible to issue an export permit for long lead-time items since delivery was scheduled after the expiry date of the act.
Therefore, industry and government obviously have been required to go to considerable lengths in such instances to provide as much reassurance as possible to potential buyers, short of a definitive commitment, that export permits will be granted. Since it is hoped that Canadian exports of long lead-time, advanced technology products will expand to state-trading nations, it would be useful to reduce administrative impediments and irritations in dealing with these potential customers to a minimum.
For these reasons I hope that hon. members will join with me in recognizing the urgency of dealing with these matters and, hopefully, will give prompt passage to the bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING EXPORT OF NATURAL RESOURCE PRODUCTS AND LIMITATION OF IMPORT OF FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is received with somewhat mixed emotions. It gives to the government a very substantial increase in its arbitrary powers, which has in fact the potential for consequences which are far beyond those that might appear inevitable in the short-run or on cursory examination. Curiously enough, the vehicle for this new broad range of powers is the Export and Import Permits Act, envisaged primarily as an act to protect the vital interests of Canadian security from a defence and security standpoint. One wonders if it is a sign of the times, based perhaps on the experience of the Arab world in using a resource, namely oil, as a strategic weapon, that we now consider raw materials in that sense or is it merely a question of expediency that an existing act is being used for the purpose of obtaining new powers with objectives far removed from those associated with the main purport of the original act.
1682

April 23, 1974
Export and Import Permits
The proposed amendments have the effect of introducing economic dirigisme with somewhat nationalistic overtones. Clause one will permit the cabinet to restrict the export of any natural resource produced in Canada if national policy requires the further processing of the product in this country. In addition, the cabinet would be permitted to restrict the export of raw or processed material other than agricultural products in circumstances of surplus supply and depressed prices.
On the agricultural side the cabinet, in addition to the powers already explicitly provided in the act, will be able to limit the import of any article under the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act similar to articles produced or marketed in Canada where the quantities are fixed or determined under the act. With the general objective of increasing the extent of processing of Canadian raw materials in Canada it is difficult to argue. This is a view which is widely held. I think Canadians are tired of being hewers of wood and drawers of water. They feel we should have a greater participation in the processing of our own raw materials. This is a perfectly legitimate aspiration of Canadians. There are many examples one can think of.
Uranium, for instance, is a natural resource which obviously will come into increased demand around the world. It is a rare commodity in the sense that it has such a vast power potential. It is, in fact, one of the great resources of the world. It can be used as a trade-off to other power sources. It will have a profound effect not only as an alternative to the burning of fossil fuels, for example, but consequently as an economic limitation of a sort to the pricing of other energy sources. It has often been suggested that we should enrich uranium in this country and take advantage of the tremendous increase in value added that that would entail. It has also been suggested we should refine more of our oil in Canada and should export, to the extent that we do export oil from this country, a higher proportion of refined and finished products, thereby ensuring a greater return to Canadian industry and greater opportunities for Canadians to participate and thereby benefit from the higher technology and techniques involved.
Some of our entrepreneurs are doing the same thing in respect of lumber. We are now developing at a very rapid rate trade in pre-fabricated houses which are being exported to France, Japan and elsewhere. One could make a case for the encouragement of a greater degree of processing of these materials, including Canadian lumber, in this country. Of course, another example where we have long complained that United States markets were not available to us to the extent they should be, is in the field of fine papers from our forest products. These are merely indicative of the types of processing opportunities which are available to us as Canadians.
There is a long list. I have not attempted to enumerate in any exhaustive way the wide variety and scope which is available to us, but have merely indicated that there are areas where we could increase the extent of processing in Canada, and consequently benefit in a very material way from the availability in this country of the vast natural resources we have. I suggest this is an area which deserves perhaps more study than we have given it, and that we

should undertake as a matter of urgency a study of the areas in which Canadian value added could be achieved, with a minimum of capital investment and a maximum return to Canadians. The whole question of resource development is a very controversial one, in respect of our renewable resources less so than when one discusses the non-renewable resources. When it comes to renewable resources I think the principles are fairly widely accepted. The principle of course is that we should manage our forests, our fisheries and our farms in such a way that we are able to optimize the yield on a sustainable basis. It is just a matter of common sense that we introduce policies that will give us, on a long term projection, the maximum yield which can be obtained without destroying the basis of the annual harvest.
We have much to learn in these areas. Our forest management techniques although quite excellent in some areas are perhaps not as good as they could be. I am sure that hon. members who are particularly interested in the fishery would say we have much to achieve in this area, including the development of international agreements which will not only enable but require our partners in the world to use the discretion necessary in order to maximize the yield on a long-term basis. But in these areas there are some established principles. The principles are really those I have stated, a maximization of the long-term sustainable yield.
When it comes to the question of non-renewable resources the determination of what one might call the best interest is not so easily made. Extreme positions range all the way from a full-speed ahead type of unlimited exploitation on the one hand, to an attitude of leave the resources in the ground for future generations and only use what is immediately required in Canada by Canadians, on the other hand. These are the extreme positions. I would suspect, as is ordinarily the case, that some middle ground would make the most sense for Canada. I urge the government once again to consider the desirability of cost-benefit studies in these areas. Seldom have I heard- as a matter of fact I have never heard-a discussion of this very important question based on sufficient information as would answer the question whether it is in Canada's long-term interest to accelerate exploitation of certain resources and to use the yield from those resources to repatriate the ownership of Canadian equities in many areas, including manufacturing facilities, as against the inevitable appreciated value of the resources if left for exploitation at some future time. I do not say that the answer to this question will be a categorical one but I do say that any good manager-and certainly this would apply in the present case in so far as a government of Canada is concerned-in order to make the decisions which are in the best interests of Canada should have that information available to him.
So, it would be very worthwhile without any further delay to have some top notch economist work out the long term benefits of Canadian equity ownership of industry, for example, and to compare what the yield would be to Canadians as consumers and as taxpayers by following different courses, whether they would realize the most benefit from an accelerated exploitation of some limited

apply pressure, direct or indirect, to extend the scope of the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act beyond that which is required or determined by the farmers themselves. They should not be subject to subtle pressure from the government or the civil service which may have its own ideas as to how things should be done.
Finally, I think the minister has made an acceptable case for the deletion of the expiry date of the act. I think its original inclusion was related to the cold war and the hope the day would come when it would not be necessary to have this kind of legislation on the books. In those circumstances, it should have a periodic review by parliament. With the kinds of powers now being asked for, and the extension of the scope of the act as to what is really an economic dirigisme, it would seem proper that the act be accepted as a permanent piece of legislation and given a fair trail. It should of course be subject to amendment at any time in the normal way, but without the consequent problems that arise from statutes with a specific expiry date.
We will support this bill, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the far-reaching consequences. We reserve the right in committee to examine in detail some of the more profound and possibly far-reaching consequences that are difficult to really come to grips with at first glance. At the same time, we think these powers are probably a legitimate extension of government in the present context and we will go along through second reading to the committee stage.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING EXPORT OF NATURAL RESOURCE PRODUCTS AND LIMITATION OF IMPORT OF FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to pick up the point with which the preceding speaker concluded his comments. He referred to the fact that the act to be amended by this bill originally came into being to deal with the armament trade. I think that is highly symbolic of the kind of situation in which Canada finds itself, whether it is governed by the Liberal party at the federal level or the Conservative party. We do not have an act directly, primarily or fundamentally concerned with resource development which is in force at the federal level. Instead, we are gradually inching our way toward some kind of resource management policy by means of amending an act that was originally passed to deal with trade in armaments. This is symptomatic of the kind of resource management we have had in Canada for many years under the Liberal government and for a brief period under the Conservative government since world war II.
What we have in Canada in terms of resources is a situation where our country is rich in resources but poor in policy. We have wealth and poverty together, poverty of ideas and programs, but rich in potential. I do not think there is another country that has allowed its resources to be plundered in the systematic way for short-range financial gain that we have permitted in this country. What has happened has been that the federal governments of Canada have taken a very short-run view. They have looked at the resources of northern Ontario, and it is interesting to note that the minister who introduced the bill is from northern Ontario, as well as similar kinds of mineral deposits in part of the prairies and from the rich resource province of British Columbia, and allowed them to be sold to the highest bidder on the world's markets.

This action provided jobs in the short-run at a faster rate than would otherwise have been the case. I think that point must be acknowledged. However, that is the sole virtue for such a policy.
Since world war II, more jobs have been created as a result of that policy than would have been the case had we adopted a sensible resource management policy which was concerned with the long-run development of Canada as an independent trading nation, and diversified the foundation of its economy by having a much higher percentage employed in the manufacturing sector.
I want to briefly outline a basic shift in policy that is required. I am speaking in terms of the general objectives of this bill. I am under no illusion. This bill in itself only deals with this question in the most peripheral way. None the less, one can take the opportunity of indicating that we really need a much broader bill, one that goes far beyond the details of this one in terms of implementing the general purpose to which the minister alluded at the outset.
The minister said that the purpose of this bill is to give manifestation of the government's concern. He said there should be a proper management of resource export policy to ensure, and I am just summarizing his words, that maximum or proper economic advantage come to Canada. That is precisely what has been neglected in the past. It has been a short-term policy rather than long-term. It is precisely the stated objectives of the minister's speech that we should be concerned about in terms of the future of Canada, especially future generations of Canadians.
What we need is a full implementation of the steps that have so far been partially implemented by this government in the life of this parliament, that is a full fledged commitment to a two price system in terms of our natural resources. We now have a two price system for agricultural products and we have a two price system for oil. We got the latter grudgingly from the government of Canada in the middle of last December. But this has had distinctly important advantages for Canada in the short-run and in the long-run. I will come back to that in a minute, Mr. Speaker.
What we need, and I want to assert this now, is an extension of the two price system beyond these two commodities, to a whole range of other commodities. I will list some of them before I suggest in a general way what the benefits would be from such a program for the people of Canada. I should like to suggest that such a two price system, one for export and one for import, be applied to energy resources-oil, natural gas, coal, uranium and hydroelectric power. In metals it should include copper, lead, zinc, gold and silver; in non-metallic minerals, gypsum, salt, asbestos, phosphates; and forest products, including lumber.
What we need at the federal level is a natural resources marketing board in each of these areas, that would take as its basic objective, the need to establish a two price system; one for Canada and Canadians and one for world exports.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING EXPORT OF NATURAL RESOURCE PRODUCTS AND LIMITATION OF IMPORT OF FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That is the Russian system!
April 23, 1974

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING EXPORT OF NATURAL RESOURCE PRODUCTS AND LIMITATION OF IMPORT OF FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I heard an interjection from somewhere saying that is the Russian system. I am not at all sure that in detail that is the Russian system. But apart from a lot of negative aspects of that society, if they have the kind of system that I am about to detail, I think it is a remarkably good idea. Just because it is in effect in a fundamentally totalitarian society like the Soviet Union, whose basic negative components all in this House would reject, is no reason we should automatically conclude that they might all be wrong. I understand, for instance, that the Soviet Union has developed good medical techniques for operating. I am certain that even certain Conservative members of parliament if they needed brain surgery-and someone has said that some of them do-would not reject techniques that were originated in the Soviet Union!
That digression aside, Mr. Speaker, I should like to go on. First of all, in terms of dealing with inflation, we want to be able to protect Canadian businessmen as well as Canadian consumers. We want to ensure that when world demand for our natural products is increasing, the price that is established at the world market level may not be the price paid to Canadian producers for that portion of the product sold to Canadian consumers. This applies directly to a number of petrochemical products.
A businessman from Montreal telephoned me about three weeks ago. He was concerned that he could not get a certain product because the multinational corporation in Canada which controlled its production was shipping it all to the United States. In this case it was not simply a matter of price, but of getting the commodity at all. As a result, part of that enterprise is going out of business and those consumers who were buying the product will no longer get it. The kind of control of resources which I have suggested would ensure that Canadian needs were met, and that related to that the price established in world markets need not be duplicated in Canada but that lower prices could be made to prevail in Canada where the natural resource is located.
The government recognizes this principle in its oil policy, as a of which they have developed, and I think sensibly, a two price system for oil: one that will meet the needs, in some sense, of the oil producing provinces to get world prices for their products and also to ensure that Canadians who have natural resources are not charged the higher world price level. So, there is that benefit. We get lower prices in terms of natural resources for Canadians and, second, we ensure that Canada's needs in terms of supply are met.
The third point I want to make is worth elaborating at greater length. It is my view that developing a two price system of this kind for natural resources in the areas I have outlined would provide the best foundation for building a competitive secondary industry in Canada. This is a much better system to ensure that Canadian secondary industry has access to commodities that we have in this country at lower prices, simply because the product is located in this country, than trying to build secondary industry either on the basis of higher tariffs which simply build in inefficiency and protect firms that are not innovative or this is the alternative approach that has been used by this government trying to encourage the development of industry in Canada by having absurdly low taxation
Export and Import Permits
levels in the corporate sector. I repeat the point: making sure that Canadian businesses have access at lower prices to Canadian resources is the best way of ensuring that we can get a manufacturing industry under way that is competitive, in world terms, in Canada. That is why an overall national strategy is essential in terms of dealing with natural resources. It is much better than a tariff policy and is much better than reducing corporation taxes to ensure an industrial growth for Canada.
Let me give an illustration from an area of the economy that I am particularly concerned about because it is in my constituency. I refer to the automotive industry. As a result of action taken by this government, we have had a significant reduction in corporation taxes to manufacturers in the last few years. This has affected my constituency directly, as it has affected many other manufacturing constituencies. But have the benefits of the special tax concessions really amounted to much? In introducing the measure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said that he wanted three things: he wanted to improve our trade and manufacturing; he wanted to increase jobs, and he wanted to see the benefits of reduced taxes passed on in the form of lower prices to consumers.
In every aspect of manufacturing, and particularly but, not exclusively automobiles, the minister's stated objectives were failures. In terms of improvement in trade, the fact is that in 1973 our manufacturing deficit increased to $6.4 billion. This is up from a deficit of $4.9 billion in the previous year and $3.7 billion in 1971. In other words, one of the objectives of reducing the corporate taxes, namely, to increase trade in manufacturing, failed. We continue to have a mounting deficit in manufacturing trade. The corporate tax reduction did nothing to alleviate that trend which is many years old and is continuing. In terms of increased employment, the fact is that in manufacturing there was an increase of some 6 per cent in jobs last year. During the same year employment in sections of our economy concerned with trade went up by 6.2 per cent and in construction, by 9.6 per cent. Again I say that the corporate tax reduction approach did not necessarily bring about any great increase in the number of employed, because in those sectors where the tax reductions did not apply, namely trade and construction, the sectors just mentioned, there was a greater increase in employment than in those sectors where the tax reduction did apply. So, the objective of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) does not seem to have materialized.
I hardly need to elaborate on the theme of price reductions for consumers. Our inflation rate now approaches the highest levels of other western economies. There has been no reduction in price. By following the route favoured by this government, that of reducing corporate taxes for the manufacturing sector of our economy-and I will not document cases because that has already been done many times by members of the NDP-you bring about increases in profits. Profits in the corporate sector are now at their highest since the Korean war. Clearly, that approach does not work. Reducing the corporate tax simply benefits those who control the corporations. That action gives them higher profits, but does not produce any net benefits which could not be exceeded by other meas-

April 23, 1974
Export and Import Permits
ures relating to other aspects of economic policy. I have just discussed those.
If we want to ensure the development of our economy, we do not need lower taxes for our corporations, nor higher tariffs to protect the inefficient; we need measures to make sure that industry in Canada will have access to our resources at prices lower than those available for the manufacturers of the United States, Japan, France and West Germany, who now purchase great amounts of our natural resources.
Let me give an example of what this means in the automotive industry. At present, a large proportion of bumpers for automobiles on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border depends very substantially on the production of Canadian nickel which comes from northern Ontario. At present, on the Canadian side of the industry we are witnessing many lay-offs because of the cutback in the production of certain automobile models in the United States. If we were to say to Canadian producers, "You can get your nickel at a lower price, establish it in Canada, than American producers can," that would mean that our firms which will compete in Canada with United States firms for contracts will be in a much better competitive position. That, it seems to me, is what can be done in almost every other aspect of Canadian manufacturing. We could give our manufacturers that sort of advantage on the basis of the resources existing in Canada. Let us not give them artificial protection by means of tariffs; let us not protect them artificially by means of lower taxes which bring negative effects for the rest of the population.
Let us give them an advantage that is appropriate in a country rich with natural resources. I gave the foregoing illustration on the basis of what I know from having studied that industry directly. If you provide nickel to Canadian producers at prices lower than you provide it for American producers, the result would be an increase on this side of the border of some thousands of jobs. The stated purpose of the bill is to give the federal government greater control over resource policy and to ensure that maximum economic benefits will accrue to Canada from resource management. Let me conclude my observations on the bill by saying that an over-all two price system such as I have just suggested for natural resources is absolutely essential. The bill, unless supplemented and fortified by such a national policy, would be almost totally useless in meeting its stated objective. It would look fine in print; it would sound splendid when ministers made speeches about it around the country; but, in terms of bringing positive benefits for the people of Canada, it will be entirely without substance.
I want to add one final point. If we establish over-all control over the export of natural resources, if we regulate the amounts of non-renewable resources in particular which can be shipped abroad, we can, at the federal level, control the rate of depletion of our non-renewable resources. We also need that kind of policy in Canada, a policy which has not been brought in because of the commitment made by the present and previous federal governments to create the greatest number of jobs in the shortest time. If we implement the kind of over-all control over natural resources which I am suggesting on behalf of my party, we would ensure for future generations in

Canada a continuing number of jobs based on important Canadian resources. Further, they will not simply be jobs in our mines and forests; they will also be jobs in our cities and towns, in the manufacturing centres.
